An introduction to monitoring

Attainment versus Growth

 Attainment-Status
 Assessing student academic performance, whether formally with a
standardized assessment of informally through observation, involves the the
 collection of data evidence that is subsequently used to draw an inference
 about the state of the student’s subject matter understanding (that is, their
 attainment-status) at that point-in time.

 Growth-Progress

As the words imply, growth-progress captures change in attainment-status
over time. When at least two observations of a student’s attainment-status
are available, it’s possible to ask the question: Did the student demonstrate
 academic growth-progress?

Attainment versus Growth

• The existence of annual student testing together with unique student
 identifiers provides multiple assessment observations for individual students
 and forms the foundation for the calculation of student growth.
• Over the last decade, most states including North Carolina have begun
 calculation of longitudinal student growth using large scale state assessments.
• The analysis of student growth is controversial primarily because of the uses to
 which it is put: Teacher & School Evaluation.

Why Student Growth?

 If you care about student
 attainment, then you care about
 student growth.
 • Where you are is a function of
 where you started and how
 quickly you’ve travelled since.
 • Student growth and student
 attainment/achievement are
 related in this way.
 • Distance = Rate x Time
 • Those who start behind tend
 to stay behind and those that
 start ahead tend to stay ahead.

Conceptual Understanding

• The concept of student growth isn’t as difficult to understand and popular
 perception suggests.
• Calculations may be complicated but knowing how to calculate student
 growth is not synonymous with understanding student growth:
 – The number π (pi=3.14159…) is difficult to calculate but is simple to
 understand conceptually.
 – Height and weight percentiles associated with children are difficult to
 calculate but are simple to understand conceptually.
• Computational details are important but often obscure a simple conceptual
 basis.

Student Growth: Introductory Concepts

 • There are 3 general approaches of calculating student growth:
 – Growth as an amount of change (i.e., gain).
 – Growth as a norm/peer referenced quantity.
 – Growth as a criterion referenced quantity.

Student Growth: Introductory Concepts

 • Growth as an amount of change:
 – What could be more simple?
 – Like height or weight just calculate the amount of change.
 – Requires a vertical scale (which North Carolina doesn’t have)
 – Growth = Score Time 2 - Score Time 1
 • Not as simple as it seems:
 – Comparisons between students often leads to wrong conclusions
 – Interpreting change requires context.

Student Growth: Introductory Concepts

 •This is analogous to height/weight measures for infants.
 •Growth amounts are tricky to interpret and require context.
 •Peer based comparisons used by growth analyses are a way to
 acquire that context.

 An infant male toddler is measured at 2 and 3 years of age and is
 shown to have grown 4 inches. The magnitude of increase—4
 inches—is a well understood quantity that any parent can grasp
 and calculate at home using a simple yardstick. However, parents
 leaving their pediatrician’s office knowing only how much their
 child has grown would likely be wanting for more information:
 Parents are not interested in an absolute magnitude of growth, but
 instead in a norm-referenced quantity locating that 4 inch increase
 alongside the height increases of similar children.

Student Growth: Introductory Concepts

• Peer-based analyses are also called norm-referenced analyses.
• Like with infant height/weight charts, peers are children/student with similar
 characteristics.
• For growth analyses using large scale assessments, peers are students with (at
 least) the same scale score history on the same tests.
• Peer based norms are invaluable in providing context for stakeholders to
 understand student growth.
• Subtraction isn’t a growth model, even when it’s permitted by a vertical scale.

Student Growth: Accountability

• Student growth is contentious largely because it is used as part of school and
 teacher evaluation.
• Much of the contention centers around claims that the quantities derived
 (usually referred to as teacher of school value-added estimates) isolate the
 contributions of teachers or schools.
• There is not universal consensus over whether such estimates isolate teacher
 of school contributions.
• At a minimum, the teacher and school value-added estimates do describe the
 average amount of learning demonstrated by students associated with the
 teacher or school.
